source_text: Dicimus sanctos Veteris Testamenti perfecta hinc iustitia ad aeternam transisse vitam, id est, studio virtutis ab omnibus recessisse peccatis, quia et illi, quos legimus aliquid peccasse, postea tamen eos emendasse cognovimus.
pass_a_gloss: We say that the saints of the Old Testament passed from here to eternal life with perfected justice: that is, by pursuit of virtue they withdrew from all sins, because even those whom we read to have sinned something, we nevertheless know afterward to have corrected themselves.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: We say that the saints of the Old Testament passed from this life to eternal life with their righteousness perfected. That is, through devotion to virtue they had turned away from all sins. For even those whom we read of as having committed some sin, we know to have corrected themselves afterward.

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (Letter to Rome, words preserved in Augustine, Contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum 1); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
